## Key decision I need from you
Do you want the app to use:

Recommendation for MVP: use a lightweight image-classifier (vision model) for Phase 0. Reason: multimodal LLMs that meaningfully interpret images are currently much larger and harder to run on-device (especially on iPhone 12 / 4 GB). A vision classifier + small rule/fusion layer (barcode/text detection + heuristics) will be compact, reliable, privacy-preserving, and easy to optimize for ANE. ## Concrete model recommendations (start points you can get from Hugging Face / GitHub)
(These are lightweight vision backbones well-suited for transfer learning and Core ML conversion; I’ll validate exact HF handles before download during implementation.)

- Primary classifier (recommended MVP):
  - EfficientNet‑Lite0 (or Lite1) — mobile-first EfficientNet variant intended for edge/mobile. Good accuracy vs compute, friendly to quantization and conversion with coremltools.
  - MobileNetV3 (Large or Small depending on budget) — proven mobile-ready backbone; easy transfer learning.
- Optional / fallback:
  - MobileViT-XXS or MobileViT-XS — hybrid conv+attention models useful if your images have high clutter (trade memory for improved generalization).
- Multi-object / scene fallback (if you later need boxes):
  - YOLOv8n (nano) — a very small detector; can be exported to Core ML and used when the scene contains multiple items.
- Retrieval / similarity fallback (no full retrain):
  - Vision feature prints (Vision framework / VNGenerateImageFeaturePrintRequest) or a tiny CLIP-like image encoder (ViT-Tiny) to do nearest-neighbor matching against a curated catalog.

I will verify exact Hugging Face model names/weights during Phase 0 (and prefer official TF/PyTorch checkpoints or authors’ repos to avoid license surprises).

## Why not an on-device LLM (for now)
- Multimodal LLMs (MiniGPT4, LLaVA, etc.) either rely on large vision or language components and are heavy for iPhone 12. Distilling/downgrading them to small models that still perform well is non-trivial and not a good fit for the MVP timeline.
- The waste-sorting task is naturally a classification problem and maps well to a compact classifier + small fusion layer (text/barcode cues). This minimizes memory, latency, and privacy surface.

## Inference contract & data shapes (what I’ll implement)
- Input: single photo taken by user → CVPixelBuffer (camera) → normalized 3-channel tensor (RGB) resized to model input (224x224 or 256x256 depending on model).
- Output: { label: String, confidence: Double } for the top-K predictions (default: top-1 and confidence).
- Inference API surface: asynchronous call with timeout and error enums: .success(label, confidence), .lowConfidence, .modelNotLoaded, .timeout, .internalError.
- Defaults: inference runs on a serial background queue; UI only reads results through main thread dispatch.

## Concrete optimizations targeted to iPhone 12 / 4GB RAM
I’ll implement these in code (and comment the Swift) so you can learn along the way:

1. Model selection + quantization
   - Use EfficientNet‑Lite0 or MobileNetV3 converted to Core ML and then quantized (8-bit/INT8 via coremltools). Quantized models have much smaller memory footprint and better ANE residency.
2. Small input size
   - Limit input resolution to the model’s recommended size (e.g., 224x224). Avoid processing full camera resolution.
3. Preallocate buffer pools
   - Use a `CVPixelBufferPool` for camera-to-model buffers to avoid repeated allocations on capture.
4. Metal-backed preprocessing
   - Use Vision + Metal / MPS for resize and normalize steps where possible to avoid copying to CPU memory.
5. Reuse VNCoreMLRequest / VNCoreMLModel
   - Create and reuse VNCoreMLModel/VNCoreMLRequest objects and keep them alive for the app’s lifetime to avoid recompile overhead.
6. Serial inference queue + single in-flight inference
   - Run inferences on a dedicated serial DispatchQueue and enforce at-most-one in-flight request to avoid memory spikes. Drop intermediate frames when busy.
7. Warm-up & model residency
   - Perform a warm-up inference on launch with a dummy tensor to ensure ANE resources are resident before user interaction.
8. Autorelease pools & explicit buffer release
   - Wrap inference work in `autoreleasepool {}` to force early Objective‑C autoreleased object drainage and call `CVPixelBufferUnlockBaseAddress` / `CVPixelBufferRelease` as needed.
9. Timeout & circuit breaker
   - If inference takes longer than a configured timeout (e.g., 1–2s), abort and present a retry; track failures to adjust behavior (e.g., fall back to lower-res or similar-image lookup).
10. Memory-pressure handling
    - Observe memory pressure notifications and gracefully cancel heavy work, release cached model references, and reload on-demand.
11. Use `MLModelConfiguration.computeUnits = .all`
    - Let Core ML pick ANE/GPU/CPU scheduling. Profile and adjust if unsupported ops force GPU fallback.
12. Minimal post-processing
    - Keep post-processing (e.g., label mapping) lightweight and non-blocking; use precomputed label lists and small lookup tables.

## Privacy & security (enforced in Phase 0)
- No raw images persist. If we need labels for retraining, upload only if user explicitly opts in and only the minimal data required (e.g., feature hash or curated sample) — but for Phase 0 we will not implement uploads.
- Local metadata encrypted at rest when stored (Keychain-derived key).
- Any code that would contact network is gated behind explicit opt-in and is disabled by default.
- Model updates (if added later) will be signed bundles validated by SHA-256 and signature checking before activation.

## UX & app flow (MVP)
- App opens → ask camera permission → show camera preview full-screen.
- User snaps photo → app preprocesses image → runs model inference → shows result screen:
  - Top label
  - Confidence
  - Recommendation: Recycle | Compost | Trash
  - “Not sure?” button to allow manual override (optional)
- Minimal UI interactions to keep code small and robust.

Below is a mid-level, practical explanation of automated Core ML conversion in CI and how we'll proceed with the Phase 0 implementation.

## High-level CI plan for model conversion (what, why)
Goal: automate the repeatable steps required to convert a public PyTorch/TensorFlow checkpoint into an optimized, signed and tested Core ML artifact (.mlmodelc) that can be bundled into the app. Automation helps avoid human errors, ensures reproducibility, and lets LLM agents make safe changes that pass CI gates.

Core steps:
1. Export source model (PyTorch/TensorFlow) into a portable format (ONNX or TFLite) — often done on Linux.
2. Run optimization/quantization using coremltools (Python) — coremltools supports conversion from ONNX/TensorFlow and includes quantization helpers.
3. Validate the converted `.mlmodel` numerically against reference inputs (run inference with PyTorch/TensorFlow and the converted model on a few synthetic test tensors).
4. Compile the `.mlmodel` into `.mlmodelc` (this step requires macOS or `xcrun` tooling) — produce the final artifact that can be shipped.
5. Run a small Core ML compatibility check (optionally `coremltools` analyzer) and upload artifacts as CI build outputs (GitHub Actions artifacts) or to a secure artifact store (S3) for later manual inspection and bundling.

Why split across OSes: conversion and quantization logic (coremltools) runs in Python and can be executed in Linux containers, but compiling `.mlmodel` to `.mlmodelc` needs Apple's `xcrun` toolchain (macOS runner) for final compilation and Apple-specific validation.

## Practical GitHub Actions flow (recommended)
- Job A (linux/pytorch): runs on ubuntu-latest
  - Install Python, PyTorch, ONNX, coremltools (for some conversions we can run coremltools here too).
  - Convert HF checkpoint → ONNX → `.mlmodel` (coremltools can produce `.mlmodel`).
  - Run quantization (8-bit) with coremltools quantization utilities.
  - Run a lightweight numerical validation: create N synthetic images (random tensors or a small curated test set), compute outputs from original model (PyTorch) and from converted `.mlmodel` via `coremltools.models.MLModel.predict`. Check that top-1 label or confidence delta is within tolerated thresholds.
  - Upload the intermediate `.mlmodel` artifact to Actions artifacts or S3.
- Job B (macos): runs on macos-latest, depends on Job A
  - Download `.mlmodel` from artifacts.
  - Use `xcrun coremlcompiler` or `xcrun mlmodelc` to compile into `.mlmodelc`.
  - Run additional Core ML checks (ensure no unsupported ops, check model size).
  - Optionally run Apple's `coremltools` analyzer requiring macOS frameworks.
  - Upload `.mlmodelc` artifact for human review or to S3 for the app to fetch during builds.

Notes:
- Keep conversion deterministic: pin Python versions and package versions in a `requirements.txt`.
- Avoid committing generated model artifacts to git. Store them as pipeline artifacts or in an artifact store (S3) protected by CI secrets.
- For Phase 0 we can keep automatic conversion as an optional step. Initially I will document the flow in `README.md` and implement a minimal GitHub Actions job that runs unit tests and validates that conversion scripts execute (without shipping full models). Later we can enable full conversion when a model checkpoint is chosen.

## Safety checks and validation thresholds
- Numeric tolerance: allow minor differences post-quantization. For classification:
  - Top-1 label match >= 95% on small validation subset (if possible).
  - Confidence delta per-sample < 0.1 absolute (tunable).
- If quantization reduces accuracy below your targets (~90% object recognition, 95% for waste-class), fail the job and mark the model unacceptable.

## Phase 0 approach (practical, incremental)
- I’ll document the conversion steps and include script templates:
  - `scripts/convert_to_coreml.py` — Python script with knobs (input HF path, output `.mlmodel`, quantize boolean).
  - `README.md` — exact commands and minimal requirements to run locally.
- Add a GitHub Actions workflow `ci/model-convert.yml` stub:
  - Stage A: check environment + run `scripts/convert_to_coreml.py --dry-run` to ensure dependencies installed.
  - Stage B (macOS): ensure `xcrun` is available and that `.mlmodel` compiles (dry-run mode or small test file).
- I'll scaffold `ModelResources/` and the CI stub during Phase 0, and implement full conversion later after we pick a checkpoint.

## License and artifact policy
- Use only Apache-2.0 / MIT / BSD-like models to avoid copyleft complications. We'll list the exact upstream license next to each candidate checkpoint.
- Don't commit large binaries to the repo. Instead use CI artifacts or S3 with signed, short-lived URLs for provisioning test builds.
